description_full: Energizer Holdings, Inc., together with its subsidiaries, manufactures, markets, and distributes household batteries, specialty batteries, and lighting products worldwide. It offers household batteries, including primary, rechargeable, specialty, and hearing aid under the Energizer, Eveready, Rayovac, and Varta brands; and protectants, wipes, tire and wheel care products, glass cleaners, leather care products, air fresheners, and washes under the Armor All, Nu Finish, Refresh Your Car!, LEXOL, Eagle One, NEVR-DULL, California Scents, Driven, Bahama & Co, Carnu, Grand Prix, Kit, Tempo, and Centralsul brands. The company also provides fuel and oil additives, functional fluids, and other performance chemical products under the STP brand; automotive air conditioning recharge products, other refrigerant and recharge kits, sealants, and accessories under the A/C PRO brand name. In addition, it distributes and markets lighting products comprising handheld, headlights, lanterns, and area lights; flashlights under the Hard Case, Dolphin, and WeatherReady brands; and licenses brands to developing consumer solutions in solar, automotive batteries, portable power for critical devices, generators, power tools, household light bulbs, and other lighting products. The company sells its products through direct sales force, distributors, and wholesalers, as well as retail locations, mass merchandisers and warehouse clubs, food, drug and convenience stores, electronics specialty stores and department stores, hardware and automotive centers, e-commerce, and military stores. Energizer Holdings, Inc. was incorporated in 2015 and is headquartered in Saint Louis, Missouri.
ceo_bio: Mr. Mark S. LaVigne J.D. | President, CEO & Director | Age 54 | Compensation: $2.4M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 6K people. Revenue per employee of $488K ranks in the above the sector median among Industrials peers, improving at 6%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Each employee generates $10K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $4K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 5× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (3/10).
financial_summary: Energizer Holdings, Inc. is a small-cap industrials business with a $1.6B market cap on $3.0B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -1% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade — essentially flat, and a business treading water is rarely a path to compounding.
Returns on capital run at 8% against a 7% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically, with gross margins sitting at 40%.

The business throws off $63M in free cash flow — roughly 2 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders. Cash conversion is thin at 0.62×, however, which raises the oldest question in analysis: are these earnings backed by cash?.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 5.6× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 2.8× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 10.8% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 13% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.

sect: Its 15% operating margin runs 6pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.35x).
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-1.3% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 544 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 8% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 46% and a beta of 0.83, it moves roughly with the market.
About $20.1M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 49% in the 2020 crash and 38% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The price sits above its blended-model fair value of $19.25 (margin of safety -24%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 59%), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 55% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 3.9% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 8.9% (vs the 8% bar).
The 6 covering analysts target $22.00 on average, 8% below the price.
prof: ROIC of 8% earns above the cost of capital of 7.0%, but the 1pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.84).
It runs a 40% gross margin and converts 2% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is a concern: cash conversion of only 0.62x.
ROE of 141% is amplified by 26.8x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
It spends 1.1% of revenue on R&D and 0.9% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 5.6x net debt to EBITDA ($236.2M of cash against $3.4B of debt), and interest cover is thin at 2.8x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.45 in the distress zone, which caps the rating at HOLD.
Working capital ties up about 130 days of sales, a drag on cash generation.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -1.1% over 3 years, 1.5% over 5 years and 6.1% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 49% of profits supports about 4.0% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -27.3% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs only 0.7x depreciation (2.8% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 3, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 12.9%, meaningful skin in the game, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only bought over the past year (37 purchases, net $16.3M bought).
It returns 10.8% a year to shareholders (5.5% in buybacks and 5.0% in dividends).
The share count has grown 0.6% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It pays out 101% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
Short interest is elevated at 10.7% of the float, 7.8 days to cover.
people: With about 6,050 employees, each generates about $488K of revenue, 1.3x the Industrials median, and productivity has risen 6.1% a year.
That works out to $10K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.4M (5x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
